name: NVIDIA B200 in HGX B200 (compute capability 10.0)
notes: Published figures, not a measurement: no device run has confirmed any of them, and none has run here. launch_ns, link_ns, memory_efficiency, occupancy_to_saturate and memory_latency_ns are assumptions, the same on every packaged card, marked as such below.

documents.datasheet: NVIDIA Blackwell datasheet (October 2025), Technical Specifications, the HGX B200 column (https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/y441155802qub41q118b2852i557jem5.pdf, linked from https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/hgx/)
documents.hgx: NVIDIA HGX platform specifications, the HGX B200 column, for eight GPUs (https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/hgx/)
documents.sms: NVIDIA Technical Blog, Boost GPU Memory Performance with No Code Changes Using NVIDIA CUDA MPS, December 2025 (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/boost-gpu-memory-performance-with-no-code-changes-using-nvidia-cuda-mps/)
documents.sections: CUDA C++ Programming Guide 12.9, section 20, Compute Capabilities, and Table 7 of arithmetic throughput (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.9.1/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html)
documents.guide: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2, Compute Capabilities, Tables 30 and 31 (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html)

source.sms: NVIDIA Technical Blog: an HGX B200's Blackwell GPUs normally have 148 SMs.
source.cores_per_sm: CUDA C++ Programming Guide 12.9, section 20.9.1, compute capability 10.x: an SM has 128 FP32 cores, 64 FP64 cores and 64 INT32 cores; Table 7 gives 128 32-bit floating-point results and 64 32-bit integer adds a clock an SM.
source.ghz: Derived: NVIDIA publishes no B200 clock; the datasheet's FP32 75 TFLOPS on 148 x 128 cores at 2 operations per fused multiply-add is 1.979 GHz.
source.dram_gbps: Datasheet, individual HGX B200 GPU: 180 GB HBM3E at 7.7 TB/s.
source.flops: Datasheet: FP32 75 TFLOPS, FP64 and FP64 tensor 37 TFLOPS. i32 is derived as the other cards' is: 64 INT32 cores an SM against 128 FP32 cores, so half of f32.
source.tensor: HGX specifications for eight GPUs, sparse, divided by eight and halved for dense: TF32 18 PFLOPS, FP16 and BF16 36, FP8 72; FP4 is given dense, 72 PFLOPS. The datasheet's individual column agrees and rounds TF32 to 2.2 PFLOPS sparse. The model reads tensor_f16; the others are recorded for a reader.
source.link_gbps: Datasheet: PCIe Gen5 128 GB/s, both directions together, so 64 GB/s each way, before protocol overhead.
source.occupancy: CUDA Programming Guide 13.4.2, Compute Capabilities, Tables 30 and 31 (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html), 10.0 column: 64 K registers, 64 warps (2048 threads) and 228 KB of shared memory an SM; the CUDA C++ Programming Guide 12.9, section 20, says for each of 8.x, 9.0, 10.x and 12.0 that the 1 KB of shared memory not made available to a thread block is reserved for system use (shared_reserved); the CUDA Occupancy Calculator allocates registers a warp at a time in units of 256 (register_unit). No limit on resident blocks per SM is applied here.
source.shared_bytes_per_clock: CUDA C++ Programming Guide: shared memory has 32 banks, each 32 bits wide a clock cycle.
source.memory_latency_ns: Assumed. NVIDIA publishes no device-memory latency and no run here has measured one; it prices only a pipeline's asynchronous copies, as the bytes in flight over this latency. Every packaged card assumes the same 500 ns.
